explanation: A cold, dark cellar feels gloomy; a bright, cosy kitchen would make the cakes look inviting.

statement: An advert for an expensive watch is set in a grand hotel with gold mirrors. The setting links the watch with wealth.
explanation: Gold mirrors and a grand hotel suggest money, so the watch seems to belong to that world.

statement: A music video is set in an empty car park at night. The setting makes the song feel cheerful and busy.
explanation: An empty car park at night feels lonely and quiet, not cheerful.

statement: A TV drama about a family farm is set mostly in a muddy yard in winter. The setting suggests farm life is easy and relaxing.
explanation: Mud and cold weather show the hard side of farming.

statement: An advert for a cleaning spray takes place in a kitchen. The woman using the spray is the setting.
explanation: The setting is the place, the kitchen; the woman is a character.

statement: In a school play poster, the actor wears a long black coat and a tall hat. His costume suggests a character from the past.
explanation: Long coats and tall hats are old-fashioned clothes, so they point to history.

statement: In a sports advert, a tennis player wears a dirty, torn shirt. Her costume makes her look perfect and spotless.
explanation: A dirty, torn shirt shows hard work, not perfection.

statement: The detective in a crime drama wears the same old brown jacket in every episode. His costume suggests he cares more about his work than about fashion.
explanation: Wearing the same old jacket every day shows that clothes don't matter much to him.

statement: A dad in a breakfast advert wears his work suit with an apron on top. His costume shows that he has a day off.
explanation: The suit shows he is going to work; the apron shows he is cooking first.

statement: In a hospital advert, the nurse's uniform is neat and clean. Her costume helps the audience see her as professional.
explanation: A neat uniform shows she is trained and doing a serious job.

statement: In a music video, a rapper wears a gold chain and a long fur coat. His costume suggests he has very little money.
explanation: Gold and fur are expensive, so the costume suggests he is wealthy.

statement: In a film poster, a girl holds a map and a torch. These props suggest she is going on an adventure.
explanation: A map and a torch are things you take on a journey into the unknown.

statement: In an advert for a bank, a man carries a briefcase. The prop suggests he is on holiday.
explanation: A briefcase is for work, so it suggests he is going to the office.

statement: At dinner, a teenager in a TV drama keeps checking her phone. The phone is a prop that shows she is not really with her family.
explanation: Looking at the phone instead of the people at the table shows her mind is somewhere else.

statement: In a cooking advert, a grandmother holds a wooden spoon. The spoon is part of her costume.
explanation: She holds and uses it, so it is a prop; costume is what she wears.

statement: A detective in a poster holds a magnifying glass. Even without words, the prop tells us his job.
explanation: A magnifying glass is linked with looking closely for clues.

statement: A boy stands with his hands deep in his pockets, looking at the floor while his friends laugh. His pose suggests he feels left out.
explanation: Looking down and hiding his hands while others laugh shows he is not part of the fun.

statement: On a book cover, a girl sits on a wall with her chin up and her arms wide open to the sky. Her pose makes her look trapped.
explanation: Arms wide open and her chin up make her look free and full of hope.

statement: A woman in a gym advert stands with her feet apart and her arms crossed. Her pose makes her look strong and ready.
explanation: Feet apart and crossed arms are a firm, solid way to stand.

statement: In a holiday advert, a man lies back on a sun bed with his eyes closed. His pose shows that he is busy and stressed.
explanation: Lying back with his eyes closed shows he is relaxed.

statement: Two friends in an advert lean on each other and laugh. Their pose suggests they have just had an argument.
explanation: Leaning on each other and laughing shows trust and friendship, not a quarrel.

statement: A toothpaste advert uses lots of white and light blue. These colours make the product feel clean and fresh.
explanation: White and light blue are linked with water, ice and cleanliness.

statement: A poster for a horror film uses black and dark red. These colours make the film seem calm and safe.
explanation: Black and dark red suggest night, danger and blood.

statement: A charity changes its poster from grey to bright yellow. The new colour could make the poster feel sadder.
explanation: Bright yellow suggests sunshine and hope; grey is the sadder colour.

statement: A salad bar uses green everywhere on its website. The colour makes the food seem unhealthy.
explanation: Green suggests fresh vegetables and good health.

statement: A film uses grey colours in the city and bright colours in the countryside. The colours suggest the main character is happier in the countryside.
explanation: The bright colours appear where life feels better for her.

statement: A football team wears red in every photo on its website. The colour has no link with the team.
explanation: Wearing the same colour every time helps fans recognise the team, so the colour becomes part of it.

statement: The main character of a cartoon advert is a slow snail that wins a race. The character teaches children not to give up.
explanation: A slow snail winning shows that trying hard matters more than being fast.

statement: In a TV advert, a grandmother teaches her grandson to cook. Only the grandson is a character.
explanation: Both people take part in the story, so both are characters.

statement: In a film trailer, one character never speaks but is always watching. This makes the audience curious about him.
explanation: A silent watcher makes us want to know who he is and what he wants.

statement: A children's book cover shows a smiling dragon sharing his sweets. The dragon is shown as a frightening character.
explanation: Smiling and sharing show the dragon is friendly.

statement: In a phone advert, the main character is a busy mum who plans her whole day on the phone. The advert wants busy parents to see themselves in her.
explanation: Showing someone like the buyer helps them imagine using the phone themselves.

statement: The main character of a video game advert wears armour and holds a shield. The character is shown as weak.
explanation: Armour and a shield show she is ready to fight and protect, so she looks strong.

statement: A magazine called "First Steps" is full of articles about prams, cots and sleep. Its audience is babies.
explanation: Babies cannot read; the magazine is for the parents who buy prams and cots.

statement: An advert for walking frames shows smiling people over seventy in a park. Its audience is probably older people and their families.
explanation: The people shown and the product both point to an older audience.

statement: A video game cover shows a huge robot fighting in a burning city. The game is probably made for very young children.
explanation: Fighting and fire suggest older players; games for young children usually look softer and safer.

statement: A TV advert for school bags is shown during cartoons on Saturday morning. The advertisers may be trying to reach business people.
explanation: Saturday morning cartoons are watched by children, so the timing is aimed at them.

statement: A poster for a university open day is put up in a primary school. The poster is in a good place to reach its audience.
explanation: University open days are for older students; primary school children are far too young.

statement: An advert for a skate park uses slang and loud music. It is trying to speak to a young audience.
explanation: Slang and loud music are styles that many teenagers enjoy.

statement: Two photos show the same head teacher. In one, the camera looks up at her; in the other, it looks down. The camera angle changes how powerful she seems.
explanation: Looking up makes a person seem bigger and stronger; looking down makes them seem smaller.

statement: A news programme films each politician from the same camera angle. This choice favours one politician over the others.
explanation: Using the same angle for everyone treats them equally, so the camera favours no one.

statement: When a superhero loses his powers, the camera angle changes from low to high. The change shows his fall.
explanation: The low angle made him look strong; the high angle now makes him look small and weak.

statement: A photographer takes a picture of a tiny kitten from directly above. The camera angle makes the kitten look fierce.
explanation: Looking down on a small animal makes it look even smaller and more helpless.

statement: A high angle shows a new pupil standing alone in a huge, crowded school hall. The shot makes him look lost.
explanation: From above, he looks tiny among the crowd, which shows how lost he feels.

statement: In a sports film, the champion is filmed from a high angle as she lifts the trophy. The angle makes her look as powerful as possible.
explanation: A high angle makes people look smaller; a low angle would make her look more powerful.

statement: A suspect in a crime drama is filmed from a high angle in a small, bare room. The angle makes him seem trapped.
explanation: Looking down on him in a small room makes him look small and stuck.

statement: A charity film uses a high angle to show children queuing for food. The angle makes the children look in control of their situation.
explanation: Looking down on them makes them look small and in need of help, not in control.

statement: A high angle of a city at night shows thousands of lights. Here the high angle shows how big the city is, not weakness.
explanation: High angles do not always show weakness; from above, a city can look huge and impressive.

statement: A film shows a tired soldier from a high angle as he sits in the mud. The audience is meant to be afraid of him.
explanation: Seen from above in the mud, he looks weak and worn out, so we feel sorry for him instead.

statement: A low angle shows a giant statue against the sky. The shot makes the statue look even bigger.
explanation: Looking up from below makes tall things seem taller and more important.

statement: A school advert films its youngest pupils from a low angle. The angle makes them look small and weak.
explanation: A low angle looks up at people and makes them look bigger and more confident.

statement: A villain is filmed from a low angle while he laughs. The shot makes him seem more frightening.
explanation: Looking up at him makes him tower over us, which adds to the threat.

statement: An election poster shows the candidate from a low angle against a blue sky. The angle is meant to make her look ordinary and small.
explanation: A low angle makes her look tall and strong, like a leader.

statement: In a basketball advert, a low angle shows a player jumping right over the camera. The shot makes the jump look even higher.
explanation: Looking up from the ground makes the jump seem higher than it is.

statement: A magazine photographs a famous chef from a low angle. The magazine is probably trying to make him look unimportant.
explanation: Looking up at him makes him look important and respected.

statement: A charity interview films a refugee girl at eye-level. The shot makes the viewer feel equal to her, not above her.
explanation: At eye-level we meet her face to face, which builds respect rather than pity.

statement: A news report films the prime minister and a nurse both at eye-level. This makes the prime minister look more important than the nurse.
explanation: Filming both at the same eye-level makes them look equal.

statement: Most TV interviews use eye-level shots. This helps the speaker look natural and easy to trust.
explanation: Eye-level feels like a normal conversation, so viewers relax and listen.

statement: When the bully finally apologises, the film switches from low angles to eye-level. The change makes him look more threatening.
explanation: At eye-level he no longer towers over us, so he looks more equal and less threatening.

statement: A long shot shows a girl walking alone across a huge empty beach. The shot makes her look lonely.
explanation: She is small in a wide, empty space, which suggests loneliness.

statement: A film would usually use a long shot when it wants us to see the tears on a character's face.
explanation: A long shot shows the whole body and the place around it; small details like tears need a close-up.

statement: A long shot at the start of a film shows a small village between mountains. It tells the viewer where the story takes place.
explanation: Long shots show the place, which helps us understand the setting.

statement: An advert for a fitness watch uses a long shot of a runner on a mountain path. The long shot shows the watch screen clearly.
explanation: From far away the watch is too small to see; the shot shows the runner and the mountain.

statement: A newsreader is filmed in a mid shot. We can see her face and her hands as she talks.
explanation: A mid shot shows a person from the waist up, so face and hands are both clear.

statement: A mid shot of a cook can show her feet and the whole kitchen floor.
explanation: A mid shot shows a person from the waist up, so we would not see her feet or the floor.

statement: Two friends talking at a table are filmed in a mid shot. The shot lets us see their faces and their body language.
explanation: From the waist up, we can see expressions and gestures at the same time.

statement: A film uses a mid shot to show a whole army marching across a field.
explanation: A whole army needs a long shot; a mid shot shows one or two people from the waist up.

statement: In a wedding photo, the bride is in focus and the guests behind her are blurred. The focus tells us who matters most.
explanation: Our eyes go to the sharp part of the picture, so the bride stands out.

statement: A photo of a busy market has one old lady in sharp focus; everyone else is blurred. The photo is mainly about the crowd.
explanation: The sharp focus makes the old lady the main subject; the blurred crowd is just around her.

statement: In a film scene, the focus moves from a boy's face to a letter on the table. The change of focus tells us the letter is important.
explanation: Moving the sharp focus guides our eyes to the next important thing.

statement: In a car advert, the car is blurred and a tree in the corner is in sharp focus. The focus will probably help us to look at the car.
explanation: Our eyes go to the sharp part, so this focus pulls attention away from the car.

statement: A horror film poster lights a face from below, leaving the eyes in shadow. The lighting makes the face look frightening.
explanation: Light from below creates strange shadows that make faces look scary.

statement: A romantic film scene is lit only by soft candlelight. The lighting makes the scene feel cold and harsh.
explanation: Soft candlelight feels warm and gentle, which suits romance.

statement: A politician is lit by bright camera flashes against a dark night. The lighting makes him the centre of attention.
explanation: Bright light on him in the dark makes him stand out from everything else.

statement: An advert for a bed shop uses bright white lighting like a hospital ward. The lighting makes the bedroom look cosy.
explanation: Bright white light feels cold and clinical; soft, warm light would make a bedroom feel cosy.

statement: A singer is lit by a single spotlight on a dark stage. The lighting can make her look alone and important at the same time.
explanation: She is the only lit person, so she is both separated from others and the centre of attention.

statement: A detective film is set in a city full of shadows and dim street lamps. The lighting makes the city feel safe.
explanation: Shadows and dim light hide things, which makes the city feel dangerous and mysterious.

statement: A football photo shows the goalkeeper with his eyes shut and his mouth wide open as the ball flies past him. His facial expression suggests he is upset.
explanation: Shut eyes and an open mouth as the ball goes in show shock and disappointment.

statement: A woman in a toothpaste advert smiles widely and shows all her teeth. Her facial expression suggests she is embarrassed about her teeth.
explanation: A wide smile that shows her teeth suggests she is proud of them.

statement: On a book cover, a girl raises one eyebrow and half smiles. Her facial expression suggests she knows a secret.
explanation: A raised eyebrow and a small smile look knowing and playful.

statement: A news photo shows a man frowning and biting his lip outside a court. His facial expression shows he is relaxed.
explanation: Frowning and biting his lip suggest worry or stress.

statement: The dog in a charity advert looks up with wide, sad eyes. The advertisers chose this facial expression to make viewers feel sorry for it.
explanation: Wide, sad eyes make the dog look helpless, so viewers want to help.

statement: A runner crosses the finish line first with a calm, blank face. His facial expression shows great joy at winning.
explanation: A calm, blank face does not show joy; it suggests he is focused or tired.

statement: Two colleagues in a job advert lean towards each other over a laptop. Their body language shows they are working together.
explanation: Leaning in shows interest and teamwork.

statement: At a press conference, the coach crosses his arms and turns away from the reporters. His body language shows he is happy to answer questions.
explanation: Crossed arms and turning away suggest he wants to avoid the questions.

statement: A film poster shows a brother and sister standing back to back with their arms folded. Their body language suggests they are not getting on.
explanation: Standing back to back with folded arms shows distance between them.

statement: A school brochure shows a teacher kneeling down to talk to a young pupil. Her body language makes her look distant and strict.
explanation: Kneeling to the pupil's height makes her look caring and easy to talk to.

statement: The singer in a music video stands tall with her shoulders back. Her body language probably shows she is nervous.
explanation: Standing tall with her shoulders back is a confident way to stand, not a nervous one.

statement: A boy in a TV drama hides behind his mum and holds on to her coat. His body language makes him look brave.
explanation: Hiding and holding on suggests he is shy or scared.

statement: The captain in a sports photo points to the badge on her shirt. The gesture shows pride in her team.
explanation: Pointing to the badge shows she is proud to play for the team.

statement: A leader in a political poster holds up both hands with his palms facing us. The gesture suggests he is hiding something.
explanation: Open palms usually suggest honesty and having nothing to hide.

statement: A charity advert ends with a girl waving at the camera. The gesture makes the viewer feel personally involved.
explanation: Waving straight at the camera feels as if she is waving to us.

statement: The hero of a film puts a finger to his lips. The gesture tells the others to speak louder.
explanation: A finger on the lips means "be quiet".

statement: A bank adviser in an advert shakes a customer's hand. The gesture suggests trust and agreement.
explanation: A handshake is a sign of a deal and of trust.

statement: A fashion advert is shot on location in a real desert instead of a studio. The location makes the clothes feel adventurous.
explanation: A real desert suggests travel and adventure, and that feeling rubs off on the clothes.

statement: A soap opera is filmed on location in a real street in Manchester. The location makes the show feel less realistic.
explanation: Filming in a real street makes the show feel more realistic.

statement: A news report is filmed on location outside the flooded school. Being there helps viewers understand how bad the flood is.
explanation: Seeing the real place gives viewers a clearer idea of the damage.

statement: A film about life in space is made in a small studio with a painted sky. The film is shot on location.
explanation: A studio with a painted sky is not a real place, so the film is not shot on location.

statement: A peace charity's poster shows a white dove. The dove is a symbol of peace.
explanation: In many cultures, white doves are linked with peace.

statement: A broken heart is drawn on a misty window in a film poster. The symbol suggests the characters are in love and happy.
explanation: A broken heart is a symbol of sadness after love goes wrong.

statement: A recycling campaign uses green arrows that go round in a circle. The symbol shows that things can be used again.
explanation: The circle of arrows suggests materials going round and being reused.

statement: In a music video, the singer opens a cage and a bird flies out. The bird is a symbol of being trapped.
explanation: The bird flying free is a symbol of freedom, the opposite of being trapped.

statement: A lion appears behind the national team on a sports poster. The lion is used as a symbol of courage.
explanation: Lions are often linked with strength and bravery.

statement: In one TV show, the teenage characters are always arguing with their parents. This gives a narrow representation of teenagers.
explanation: Showing only arguments leaves out many other sides of teenage life.

statement: A magazine article about farming uses one photo: an old man on a tractor. The photo represents the young farmers in the article well.
explanation: An old man on a tractor leaves out the young farmers the article talks about.

statement: A film shows a wheelchair user as a funny, clever detective. The film gives disabled people a positive representation.
explanation: She is shown as clever and skilled, not as someone to pity.

statement: The local news only shows teenagers when there is a fight in town. The representation of teenagers in this news is balanced.
explanation: Only showing fights leaves out the ordinary, positive things teenagers do.

statement: Two adverts sell the same football boots. One shows a girl scoring; the other shows only boys. The representation of who plays football is different in each advert.
explanation: One includes girls as players; the other leaves them out.

statement: In a cartoon, the three scientists are young women with the same red hair and the same white coats. The cartoon represents scientists as a varied group.
explanation: Three people who look almost the same is a narrow picture; scientists are many ages and genders.

statement: A clothing brand represents its older customers as stylish and active. The brand wants older people to feel included.
explanation: Showing them as stylish suggests the clothes are for them too.

statement: A newspaper represents a group of protesters as "a mob". The word makes them sound calm and peaceful.
explanation: "Mob" suggests an angry, violent crowd.

statement: In a video game, the women characters are represented as leaders who make the big decisions. This goes against an old idea that men should lead.
explanation: Showing women in charge challenges the idea that leaders are always men.

statement: A school website represents the school only through photos of its new sports hall. The website gives a clear picture of the school's lessons.
explanation: Only showing the sports hall leaves out lessons and teachers.

statement: In a sitcom, the only teenager is lazy, rude and always on her phone. The show uses a stereotype of teenagers.
explanation: It shows a fixed, simple idea about teenagers instead of a real person.

statement: A TV advert shows a dad changing nappies and cooking dinner while the mum fixes the car. The advert repeats a stereotype about men and women.
explanation: It goes against the old stereotype that only women care for babies and only men fix cars.

statement: A film's only scientist is an old man with wild hair who forgets everything. This character is a stereotype.
explanation: The "mad scientist" is a familiar, simple type, not a real person.

statement: A cartoon shows a grandmother who goes skydiving and plays video games. The character fits the usual stereotype of grandmothers.
explanation: The usual stereotype is quiet and gentle; this grandmother goes against it.

statement: An advert shows every Asian student at the top of the class. Even though it sounds positive, this is still a stereotype.
explanation: A positive fixed idea still treats a whole group as if everyone in it were the same.

statement: The same joke appears in every episode of a comedy: the blonde character never understands anything. The joke challenges a stereotype.
explanation: It repeats the stereotype that blonde women are not clever.

statement: An advert for a skate park speaks only to teenagers. Teenagers are the social group the advert is aimed at.
explanation: The advert shows and talks to young people of a certain age.

statement: A TV report calls "people who live in the countryside" a social group. This is wrong, because people in a social group must share the same job.
explanation: People can share where they live, their age, their religion or their job; any of these can make a social group.

statement: A campaign about women in science shows female engineers, doctors and coders. The campaign wants to change how this social group is seen.
explanation: It shows women in science doing many different jobs, against the idea that science is for men.

statement: A news story says that young people don't care about the environment. The story shows the real variety inside this social group.
explanation: It treats all young people as the same and ignores the many who do care.

statement: In an old cereal advert, the mum always cooks and the dad always reads the paper. The advert gives men and women very fixed roles.
explanation: Each person has the same job every time, based only on whether they are a man or a woman.

statement: In a film, the youngest child saves the family from a fire. Her role in the story is small and unimportant.
explanation: Saving the family makes her role central to the story.

statement: A hospital drama shows a male nurse and a female surgeon working side by side. The drama suggests that jobs need not depend on gender.
explanation: Both people do jobs that go against old ideas about who does what.

statement: In a superhero film, the woman's only role is to be rescued at the end. She plays an active role in the story.
explanation: Waiting to be rescued is a passive role; she does not act for herself.

statement: In a music video, a singer moves between Chinese and English and wears clothes from both cultures. The video shows that her identity includes both.
explanation: Mixing both languages and styles shows that both cultures are part of who she is.

statement: An athlete in a sports advert has her face painted with her country's flag. The flag has nothing to do with her identity.
explanation: The flag shows she sees her country as part of who she is.

statement: A school prospectus shows pupils in their own clubs: chess, dance, robots and football. It suggests that each pupil has their own identity.
explanation: Showing different interests suggests each pupil is an individual.

statement: A clothing advert says "Be yourself", but every model wears exactly the same outfit. The advert celebrates different identities.
explanation: Everyone looks the same, which works against the message about being different.

statement: An advert for a new phone game is shown on a children's TV channel at 4 p.m. Children are its target audience.
explanation: The channel and the time are chosen to reach children after school.

statement: A magazine called "Retire Right" has articles about pensions and slow travel. Its target audience is teenagers.
explanation: Pensions and retirement suggest older adults near the end of their working lives.

statement: A perfume advert shows a glamorous woman at a party in Paris. The target audience may include women who would like that kind of life.
explanation: The advert sells a dream lifestyle that its audience would like to have.

statement: A toy shop's advert is shown late at night during a horror film. The timing will help it reach its target audience.
explanation: Children are asleep late at night and horror films are for adults, so the timing misses them.

statement: A new gym's leaflet says "Never too late to start" and shows people over sixty. Older people are part of the target audience.
explanation: The words and pictures speak directly to older people.

statement: A website selling cheap student flats promises "luxury living for top business people". The words match its target audience.
explanation: Students on a budget are not "top business people", so the words miss the audience.

statement: A charity film ends with the words "What will you do?" The question speaks directly to the viewer.
explanation: "You" addresses the person watching and asks them to act.

statement: A horror film shows the monster through the victim's eyes. The viewer sees the scene from the monster's point of view.
explanation: We see through the victim's eyes, so we share the victim's fear, not the monster's view.

statement: A furniture catalogue shows a teenager's bedroom with a made bed, neat books and a single plant. The photographer has constructed a tidy, calm image of teenage life.
explanation: Every detail has been chosen and arranged; real teenage bedrooms are rarely this neat.

statement: A news photographer waits two hours for the moment a protester raises his fist against the sunset. Because the moment really happened, the image has not been constructed.
explanation: Choosing when to shoot, what to include and which frame to publish is still constructing an image, even of a real moment.

statement: A documentary about a school uses no actors and no script. This means it is a direct copy of reality rather than a construction.
explanation: Even without actors, choices about filming, editing and music build a particular picture of the school.

statement: A fashion shoot spends six hours on lighting, make-up and editing to create a "natural morning" look. The natural look is a construction.
explanation: The effortless look took hours of planning, so it is built rather than natural.

statement: An influencer posts a photo captioned "No filter, just woke up". The caption proves the image is not a construction.
explanation: The pose, the angle and the decision to post are all choices, whatever the caption claims.

statement: In a crime drama, the hacker is a pale young man in a hoodie who never leaves his dark bedroom. The character is stereotypical.
explanation: He fits a familiar, fixed picture of a hacker instead of being an individual.

statement: A sitcom's Italian restaurant owner is a quiet accountant who hates pasta. The character is stereotypical.
explanation: He goes against the usual fixed picture of Italians as loud and food-loving.

statement: An advert for cleaning products shows only women cleaning and only men relaxing. The advert's roles are stereotypical.
explanation: It repeats a fixed idea about who does the housework.

statement: A newspaper writes "Gamers are lonely and unfit" after interviewing three players. This is a careful conclusion based on strong evidence.
explanation: Three players cannot speak for millions; the claim is a generalisation.

statement: A magazine article says "Students today can't concentrate" without giving any figures. The article makes a generalisation.
explanation: It claims something about all students with no evidence.

statement: A report says "Some young drivers take risks, but most drive safely." This sentence is a generalisation about all young drivers.
explanation: It separates "some" from "most", so it avoids treating every driver the same.

statement: A card for a baby girl says "Little Princess" and a card for a baby boy says "Little Explorer". The cards repeat a gender stereotype.
explanation: They suggest girls should be pretty and boys adventurous from the day they are born.

statement: A science museum poster shows a girl building a rocket while her brother bakes a cake. The poster repeats a gender stereotype.
explanation: Swapping the usual activities goes against the stereotype instead of repeating it.

statement: A car advert shows a woman struggling to park while two men watch and laugh. The joke relies on a gender stereotype.
explanation: It depends on the fixed idea that women are bad drivers.

statement: A bank advert shows a grandmother calmly using her phone to send money abroad. The advert relies on an age stereotype.
explanation: The stereotype would be that older people struggle with technology; she goes against it.

statement: A teen drama shows every adult as boring, strict and unable to understand young people. The drama uses an age stereotype.
explanation: It treats all adults as the same fixed type.

statement: A cartoon set in Japan shows a girl who is loud in class, bad at maths and in love with heavy metal. The character is a cultural stereotype.
explanation: She goes against the stereotype of the quiet, studious Japanese pupil.

statement: In an action film, every Russian character is a cold, silent villain. The film relies on a cultural stereotype.
explanation: It gives one fixed type to everyone from one country.

statement: A travel advert for Scotland shows a businesswoman giving a talk in a modern Glasgow office. The advert relies on the cultural stereotype of bagpipes and kilts.
explanation: There are no bagpipes or kilts; the advert shows modern working life instead.

statement: A documentary follows a refugee doctor retraining to work in a British hospital. It gives a positive representation of refugees.
explanation: It shows a refugee as skilled, hard-working and contributing.

statement: A charity advert shows homeless people only as dirty and helpless. This is a positive representation because it raises money for them.
explanation: The aim may be good, but showing them only as helpless is a negative, limited representation.

statement: A show in which every teenager is polite, clever and kind gives a positive representation, but not a realistic one.
explanation: It is flattering, but real teenagers are far more varied than that.

statement: A local newspaper runs a story about a teenager who saved a drowning child. The story gives a negative representation of young people.
explanation: Praising a brave teenager is a positive representation.

statement: A TV report shows football fans only throwing bottles and shouting at the police. The report gives a negative representation of fans.
explanation: It shows only bad behaviour and leaves out the ordinary fans.

statement: A film shows a teacher who is strict but fair and helps a struggling pupil to pass her exams. This is a negative representation of teachers.
explanation: Strict but fair and helpful is a mostly positive picture.

statement: A sports brand's poster shows runners of different ages, sizes and skin colours. The brand wants to show diversity.
explanation: Including many different kinds of people shows diversity.

statement: A company's website says "We celebrate diversity" above a photo of ten young men in identical suits. The photo supports the claim.
explanation: Ten similar young men show very little diversity, so the photo works against the words.

statement: A children's book series includes a girl with a hearing aid, a boy with two dads and a twin who uses a wheelchair. The series shows diversity without making it the main story.
explanation: The characters are varied, and their differences are simply part of everyday life in the books.

statement: A news report on a new airport quotes three people who support it and three who oppose it. The report shows bias.
explanation: Giving both sides equal space suggests the report is balanced.

statement: A sports website calls its own team's win "brilliant" but the other team's win "lucky". The website shows bias.
explanation: It describes the same kind of result differently depending on which team won.

statement: A documentary about nurses follows one nurse, Amira, in detail through a week of night shifts. It treats nurses as a crowd rather than as individuals.
explanation: Following one named person in detail shows her as an individual.

statement: A charity campaign tells the story of one named child instead of quoting big numbers. Focusing on an individual can make viewers care more.
explanation: A single person's story is easier to feel for than a large figure.

statement: A war film shows soldiers only as rows of helmets and boots. This makes each soldier feel like a distinct individual.
explanation: With no faces or names, they become a mass, not individuals.

statement: A photo of a politician is framed so that only his raised fist and open mouth are visible. The framing can make him look aggressive.
explanation: Cutting out the crowd and the context leaves only the fist and the shout.

statement: A news photo of a protest is framed tightly around twenty people, leaving out the thousands behind them. The framing makes the protest look bigger.
explanation: Tight framing on a small group makes the protest look smaller than it was.

statement: In a horror film, the frame shows a girl on one side and an empty doorway on the other. The framing makes the audience watch the doorway.
explanation: Leaving empty space around the door makes us expect something to appear there.

statement: A film poster places the hero small in the bottom corner and the villain huge in the centre. The composition suggests the hero is in control.
explanation: The villain dominates the picture, which suggests he holds the power.

statement: A bank advert's family photo places the grandparents in the centre with the children around them. The composition suggests the grandparents hold the family together.
explanation: Being at the centre, with others gathered round, makes them the heart of the group.

statement: In a magazine photo, two rivals stand at opposite edges with empty space between them. The composition suggests they are close friends.
explanation: The empty space between them suggests distance and rivalry.

statement: A film about a cold, unhappy marriage uses a palette of greys and pale blues. The colour palette matches the mood of the story.
explanation: Cold colours reflect the lack of warmth between the characters.

statement: A children's TV show uses a colour palette of bright reds, yellows and greens. The palette makes the show feel serious and adult.
explanation: Bright primary colours feel playful and young.

statement: A luxury chocolate brand uses black and gold on its packaging. The colour palette suggests the chocolate is expensive.
explanation: Black and gold are linked with elegance and wealth.

statement: A crime drama interviews a suspect under warm, golden lighting. Lighting like this usually makes a room feel threatening.
explanation: Warm, golden light feels comfortable and safe, not threatening.

statement: A furniture advert lights a living room with warm lamps at dusk. The warm lighting makes the room feel like home.
explanation: Soft, warm light suggests comfort and family.

statement: A family's kitchen has warm lighting in the happy flashbacks and cold lighting in the present day. The change of lighting suggests that life has become harder.
explanation: Warm light belongs to the happy past; cold light marks the difficult present.

statement: A holiday advert shows a beach café under cold, blue-white lighting. Cold lighting like this often makes a café feel warm and friendly.
explanation: Cold lighting feels distant; warm light would suit a holiday.

statement: A science fiction film uses cold lighting inside the spaceship. The lighting makes the ship feel clean, technical and unwelcoming.
explanation: Blue-white light suggests machines rather than comfort.

statement: A documentary about a hospital at night uses cold lighting in the corridors. The lighting is chosen to make the hospital feel cosy.
explanation: Cold light makes the corridors feel lonely and tense.

statement: A character keeps a dead plant on her desk until the final scene, when she replaces it with a new one. The plants carry symbolism about her life.
explanation: The dead plant suggests her life is stuck; the new one suggests a fresh start.

statement: A poster for a film about escape shows an empty birdcage with its door open. The symbolism suggests the character is still trapped.
explanation: An open, empty cage suggests escape and freedom.

statement: A clock that stopped at the moment of an accident appears again and again of a drama. The repeated clock adds symbolism about time standing still.
explanation: The stopped clock suggests the characters cannot move on.

statement: An advert calls its sofa "affordable" instead of "cheap". The two words have the same connotations.
explanation: "Cheap" can suggest poor quality; "affordable" sounds positive.

statement: A perfume is named "Midnight". The name has connotations of mystery and romance.
explanation: Midnight suggests darkness, secrets and late, romantic evenings.

statement: One newspaper describes a politician as "stubborn" and another calls her "determined". The words describe the same behaviour but have different connotations.
explanation: "Stubborn" sounds negative; "determined" sounds positive.

statement: A poster shows a broken pencil. The literal meaning of the image is that the writer has given up.
explanation: Literally, it is just a broken pencil; the idea of giving up is what it suggests.

statement: A headline says "Prices go through the roof". The writer wants readers to take the words at their literal meaning.
explanation: The writer means prices have risen sharply; nobody thinks a roof has been damaged.

statement: A school poster shows an empty desk with a pile of untouched homework on it. The implied meaning is that a pupil is missing lessons.
explanation: Nothing is said directly; the empty desk and homework make us work out the message.

statement: A diet advert says "Summer is coming. Are you ready?" over a photo of a beach. The advert has no implied meaning.
explanation: It implies that you need to lose weight before you can wear beach clothes.

statement: A husband in a film says "I'm fine" while slamming the cupboard doors. The implied meaning is that he is angry.
explanation: His actions contradict his words, so we understand he is upset.

statement: A nature presenter whispers to the camera, "Look closely: she's about to strike." This is not direct address because the presenter is whispering.
explanation: She is still speaking straight to the viewer, so it is direct address, however quietly.

statement: A recruitment poster shows a soldier pointing at the viewer with the words "Your country needs you". The poster uses direct address.
explanation: The pointing finger and "you" speak straight to the person looking.

statement: In a film, the characters talk only to each other and never look at the camera. The film uses direct address throughout.
explanation: Direct address means speaking to the audience; here the characters speak only to each other.

statement: A charity leaflet says "Every night, frightened children go to bed hungry." The leaflet uses emotive language.
explanation: "Frightened" and "hungry" children are chosen to make readers feel pity.

statement: A weather report says "Temperatures will reach 31 degrees on Thursday." The report uses emotive language.
explanation: It gives plain facts, with no words chosen to stir feelings.

statement: A tabloid headline calls a storm "a monster that ripped through our town". The emotive language makes the storm sound alive and frightening.
explanation: "Monster" and "ripped" turn the storm into a violent creature.

statement: One newspaper says the council "spent" £2 million on a park; another says it "wasted" £2 million. The two word choices give the same impression.
explanation: "Wasted" says the money was badly used; "spent" is neutral.

statement: A shampoo advert describes the product as "gentle" rather than "weak". The word choice makes the same quality sound like a good thing.
explanation: "Gentle" sounds caring; "weak" would sound like a fault.

statement: A report calls a group of teenagers "a gang" instead of "a group of friends". The word choice may make readers suspicious of them.
explanation: "Gang" suggests crime and danger; "friends" does not.

statement: A campaign poster repeats the word "Vote" five times. The repetition makes the message weaker.
explanation: Repeating a word makes the message stronger and harder to forget.

statement: An advert plays its jingle three times in thirty seconds. The repetition probably makes the brand harder to remember.
explanation: Hearing the same tune again and again makes the brand stick.

statement: A film shows the same red balloon in four key scenes. The repetition suggests the balloon is not important.
explanation: Repeating an image makes us notice it, so the balloon is likely to matter.

statement: Most action film posters show the hero in the centre, an explosion behind him and a huge title. These are conventions of action film posters.
explanation: These features appear again and again, so audiences expect them.

statement: A horror film poster uses pastel colours, a sunny garden and a smiling family. The poster follows what horror posters usually do.
explanation: Horror posters usually use darkness and fear; this one breaks the conventions.

statement: A news broadcast begins with dramatic music, a presenter at a desk and the main headlines. These conventions tell viewers that serious news is about to begin.
explanation: Audiences recognise these features and expect important information.

statement: A supermarket advert shows a mother checking every price and choosing a cheaper brand. The advert treats her as a careless consumer.
explanation: Comparing prices shows she is a careful consumer.

statement: A streaming service records what each user watches in order to suggest new shows. It treats viewers as consumers whose choices can be measured.
explanation: Tracking choices shows the company sees viewers as customers to keep.

statement: A clothing brand's advert shows a teenager buying a new jacket week after week. The advert encourages viewers to see themselves as consumers.
explanation: It presents buying often as normal and desirable.

statement: A toy advert uses a famous footballer to sell a plastic football. The footballer is chosen because he has no appeal to children.
explanation: Children who like football admire him, which is why he was chosen.

statement: A car advert for young drivers uses fast music and bright city lights at night. These choices are designed to appeal to young people.
explanation: Energetic music and city nightlife are aimed at a young audience.

statement: A museum replaces long text panels with touch screens and quizzes. The change will probably engage young visitors less.
explanation: Touch screens and quizzes usually engage young visitors more.

statement: A podcast asks listeners to send in their own stories each week. This helps to engage its audience.
explanation: Asking listeners to take part involves them in the show.

statement: A video begins with three minutes of silent black screen. This opening is designed to engage viewers straight away.
explanation: A silent black screen is likely to make viewers click away.

statement: A drama follows a new student through her nervous first week at a big school. Many Year 7 pupils may identify with her.
explanation: Many of them have just been through the same experience.

statement: A film's hero is a billionaire with three private jets. Most ordinary teenagers can easily identify with his everyday life.
explanation: His life is very far from theirs, so identifying with it is hard.

statement: A video game lets players choose the hero's face, voice and name. These choices help players identify with the hero.
explanation: Making the hero like yourself helps you feel you are in their place.

statement: A road-safety advert shows the moments before a car crash, then cuts to black. The intended audience response is laughter.
explanation: The advert wants shock and fear, so that viewers drive more carefully.

statement: A charity advert ends with a phone number and the words "Text GIVE now". The advert wants a response from the audience, not just feelings.
explanation: It asks viewers to act by giving money.

statement: Two people watch the same comedy: one laughs, the other is offended. This shows that one of them must have misunderstood it.
explanation: People can understand a text perfectly and still respond differently, because of their own experiences.

statement: A cooking show shows the chef burning the onions and losing her temper. The show gives an idealised picture of cooking.
explanation: Burnt food and a lost temper show the messy side; an idealised picture would look perfect.

statement: A wedding magazine shows sunny skies, perfect dresses and smiling guests page after page. It offers an idealised picture of weddings.
explanation: Real weddings have rain, stress and arguments; these pages leave them out.

statement: A university brochure shows only students working late in a crowded library with tired faces. The brochure presents an idealised student life.
explanation: Tired faces in a crowded library are realistic, not idealised.

statement: A comedy series shows a family arguing over the TV remote and running late for school. Many viewers find it relatable.
explanation: These are ordinary moments that many families share.

statement: A vlogger posts only from luxury hotels and first-class flights. Most of her young followers find her daily life relatable.
explanation: Most young people do not live like that, so her life is aspirational, not relatable.

statement: A mental-health campaign uses real teenagers talking about exam stress. The campaign wants to be relatable to students.
explanation: Real young people describing a shared worry make the message feel close to home.

statement: An advert for a budget supermarket shows a crowded car park and long queues at the tills. The advert is aspirational.
explanation: Crowds and queues are not a life people dream of; aspirational adverts show one they do.

statement: A sports drink advert shows a teenager training before dawn and later winning a final. The advert is aspirational.
explanation: It shows success that young athletes would like to achieve.

statement: A soap opera shows a family in a small flat, worrying about rent and arguing about chores. The soap opera aims to be realistic.
explanation: Ordinary money worries and chores reflect real life.

statement: An advert shows a cleaning spray removing a stain in one second, with sparkles. The advert's picture of cleaning is realistic.
explanation: Instant results with sparkles are exaggerated for effect.

statement: A Christmas advert shows a grandmother cooking, children opening presents and a dad carving the meat. The advert shows traditional family roles.
explanation: These roles follow long-standing ideas about who does what at home.

statement: A wedding advert shows two brides dancing at a beach party. The advert shows a very traditional wedding.
explanation: Two brides at a beach party go against traditional wedding images.

statement: In most car adverts the driver is a confident man, and any woman sits in the passenger seat. This is the dominant representation of driving in car adverts.
explanation: It is the most common pattern, repeated so often that it seems normal.

statement: One new film shows a female astronaut leading a mission. Because of this film, women leaders are now the dominant representation of astronauts.
explanation: A single film cannot change what is most common; the usual image is still male.

statement: Nurses are shown mainly as women in films and TV. This dominant representation can make male nurses seem unusual, even though there are many of them.
explanation: Repetition makes the common image feel like the normal one.

statement: A sports brand shows a disabled athlete in one advert out of fifty. Disability is the dominant representation in the brand's campaigns.
explanation: One advert in fifty is rare; it is far from dominant.

statement: Most city crime dramas show young Black men as suspects. A drama that makes a young Black man the calm, brilliant detective offers an alternative representation.
explanation: It shows the same group in a role the usual pattern leaves out.

statement: A new reality show follows rich young people shopping and partying, like many shows before it. It offers an alternative representation of wealthy youth.
explanation: It repeats the familiar picture rather than offering a different one.

statement: A sports magazine puts a female weightlifter on its cover, muscles and all. This is an alternative representation of female athletes.
explanation: It shows strength rather than the usual focus on slim, graceful women.

statement: A sitcom's teenager is calm, polite and loves gardening. Because she is so unusual, she reflects the dominant representation of teenagers.
explanation: She is unusual compared with the common image, so she is an alternative representation.

statement: A cereal advert shows a dad who burns the toast and cannot find the children's shoes. The dad is a counter-stereotype.
explanation: The clumsy, useless dad is a familiar stereotype, so he fits it rather than going against it.

statement: A video game makes its toughest warrior a seventy-year-old grandmother. She is a counter-stereotype.
explanation: She deliberately goes against the fixed idea that older women are frail.

statement: A female hero who is never allowed to make a mistake may go against one stereotype but become a new kind of fixed type.
explanation: Going against one stereotype can create another simple, unreal image.

statement: An advert for a cleaning product shows a woman happily mopping while her husband watches football. The advert uses a counter-stereotype.
explanation: It follows the stereotype that housework belongs to women.

statement: Of forty presenters on a TV channel, one has a visible disability. Disabled people are under-represented on the channel.
explanation: One in forty is far fewer than the share of disabled people in society.

statement: A children's bookshop finds that half its picture books have girl heroes. Girls are under-represented as heroes in this shop's books.
explanation: Half is roughly equal, so girls are not under-represented here.

statement: A city's news website covers sport, business and crime, but rarely mentions its large Polish community. The community is under-represented.
explanation: A large group that rarely appears is shown far less than its numbers suggest.

statement: Older women do appear in a magazine's adverts, but only to sell walking sticks and pills. Because they appear at all, they cannot be under-represented.
explanation: Appearing rarely and in a narrow role is still under-representation.

statement: Nine out of ten scientists in a set of school textbooks are men. Women are over-represented in these textbooks.
explanation: Women are under-represented; it is men who are over-represented.

statement: In a week of crime news, young men appear in most stories, far more than their real share of crimes. They are over-represented in crime news.
explanation: They appear more often than real figures would suggest.

statement: A breakfast TV show's guests are mostly London business owners. London voices are over-represented on a national show.
explanation: One city's voices are heard more than its share of the country.

statement: A fashion brand uses models of many sizes, but slim models still appear in most of its photos. Larger models are over-represented.
explanation: Slim models appear most, so it is they who are over-represented.

statement: A football club's highlights video shows all four of its goals and none of the other team's five. The video is selective.
explanation: Leaving out the other team's goals gives a misleading picture of the match.

statement: A tourist brochure for a seaside town shows its beach, its harbour, its closed shops and its empty high street. The brochure is selective in showing only the best side.
explanation: It includes the closed shops and empty street, so it is not just showing the best side.

statement: A charity film about a village shows the broken well but not the new school next to it. The film is selective.
explanation: It chooses the details that support its message and leaves out others.

statement: A news report on a protest uses footage of the one moment a window was smashed. Because the footage is real, the report cannot be selective.
explanation: Real footage can still be selective if it shows one moment out of hours.

statement: Viewers watch a royal wedding through cameras chosen by the broadcaster. Their experience of the wedding is mediated.
explanation: They see only what the broadcaster chooses to show.

statement: A live football match on TV usually isn't mediated, because it is happening at that very moment.
explanation: Even live, the director chooses angles, replays and commentary, so it is mediated.

statement: A teenager learns about a war only through social media posts. Her understanding of the war is mediated by the people who posted.
explanation: She sees the war through other people's choices, not directly.

statement: A celebrity posts a photo of herself on her own account. Because she chose it herself, the photo is unmediated.
explanation: Choosing, editing and posting the photo are all choices that shape it, so it is still mediated.

statement: Years of adverts showing women shaving their legs may normalise the idea that body hair on women is wrong.
explanation: Repeating one image makes it seem like the only acceptable way.

statement: A soap opera shows a family where the mum works and the dad stays at home, episode after episode for ten years. This will probably make the arrangement seem stranger to viewers.
explanation: Showing it again and again makes it seem more normal, not stranger.

statement: A video game rewards players for violence in every level. The game may normalise violence.
explanation: Repeated rewards make violence feel like an ordinary part of play.

statement: A single advert shows a man crying at a wedding. One advert is enough to normalise men crying in public.
explanation: Normalising needs repetition across many texts; one advert is only a start.

statement: A crime drama puts its only disabled character at the centre of the poster, but gives her one line and never mentions her again. This could be described as tokenism.
explanation: She is visible enough to signal diversity but given no depth or story of her own.

statement: A school prospectus features one pupil from each year group, each with a quote about their favourite subject. This is probably tokenism.
explanation: Each pupil has a voice and a purpose; tokenism means including someone only to look fair.

statement: A boy band adds one female dancer to its video, but she appears only in the background for three seconds. The choice suggests tokenism.
explanation: Her tiny, silent role suggests she is there to look inclusive.

statement: A film includes three Asian characters, each with their own storyline and goals. The film is guilty of tokenism.
explanation: Characters with full stories are not tokens; tokenism gives people no real role.

statement: A documentary about a factory closure films the workers at home with their children and the owner only behind his desk. This positions the audience to side with the workers.
explanation: We see the workers' family lives, so we feel more for them than for the owner.

statement: A news report shows a protest only from behind police lines. The audience is positioned to see the protest from the protesters' point of view.
explanation: Filming from the police side positions us with the police.

statement: A horror film shows the killer's view through the eyeholes of his mask. The audience is uncomfortably positioned to see through the killer's eyes.
explanation: The point-of-view shot puts us in his place.

statement: A charity advert shows a hungry child's face in close-up and asks "Will you help?" The audience is positioned as a neutral observer.
explanation: The close-up and the question position us as someone who can and should help.

statement: Fans of a TV series write their own stories about minor characters and post them online. They are acting as an active audience.
explanation: They interpret and add to the text rather than simply receiving it.

statement: A class discusses a perfume advert and decides it is ridiculous. The students are behaving as a passive audience.
explanation: Questioning and judging the advert is what an active audience does.

statement: The idea of an active audience suggests that two viewers may take different meanings from the same advert.
explanation: Each person interprets the text in their own way.

statement: A boy watches six hours of TV a day without ever questioning it. This makes him an especially active audience.
explanation: Watching a lot is not the same as thinking about what you watch.

statement: A newspaper warns that children will copy every violent act they see in games. The newspaper sees children as a passive audience.
explanation: It assumes children simply absorb what they see without thinking.

statement: A teacher believes her students can spot a misleading advert and laugh at it. She sees them as a passive audience.
explanation: Believing they can question adverts treats them as active.

statement: The passive audience idea is often used to argue for banning certain films. Its critics say it underestimates viewers.
explanation: It treats audiences as easily influenced, which many people dispute.

statement: Fans who vote for contestants on a talent show are acting as a passive audience.
explanation: Voting changes the show, so they are taking part actively.

statement: A war film was praised in one country and banned in another. Its reception depended on where it was shown.
explanation: Different audiences, with different histories, received it very differently.

statement: A comedy that was popular in 1985 is attacked as offensive in 2025. This proves that the film itself has changed.
explanation: The film is the same; its reception has changed because audiences have changed.

statement: An advert went viral, but many viewers shared it in order to mock it. Its reception was not what the brand hoped for.
explanation: Being shared widely is not the same as being liked.

statement: Everyone in one cinema laughed at the same scene. This shows that a film's reception is always the same for everyone.
explanation: One shared reaction does not show that all audiences will always respond alike.

statement: A magazine's chatty mode of address, full of "you" and jokes, feels like a friend talking.
explanation: It speaks to readers informally, as an equal.

statement: A government leaflet says "Residents are advised to remain indoors." Its mode of address is chatty and friendly.
explanation: It is formal and impersonal, using "residents" rather than "you".

statement: A children's TV presenter kneels to the camera and asks "Are you ready?" The mode of address treats viewers as part of the show.
explanation: Questions and eye-level contact invite young viewers to join in.

statement: A bank's advert speaks in slang and fast jokes. This mode of address will probably make the bank seem more serious and trustworthy.
explanation: Slang and jokes make it informal; banks usually choose a calm, formal tone to seem trustworthy.

statement: A football club's website uses "we" and "our" in every match report. The mode of address makes fans feel part of the club.
explanation: "We" includes the reader as one of the team.

statement: A report says "The new stadium holds 40,000 people." This statement is subjective.
explanation: It is a fact that can be checked.

statement: A review calls a new film "the most moving story of the year". The review is subjective.
explanation: "Most moving" is a personal feeling, not something that can be measured.

statement: A photographer chooses to show a march from a low angle at dawn. Even a photo can be subjective, because it reflects her choices.
explanation: Her choice of angle and time shapes what the viewer feels.

statement: A blogger writes "In my opinion, the advert is sexist." Because she says "in my opinion", her statement is objective.
explanation: "In my opinion" signals a personal view, which is subjective.

statement: A report gives the number of people injured and the times of the accident, with sources. The report aims to be objective.
explanation: Checked facts with sources are what objective reporting looks like.

statement: A newspaper calls a politician "a disgrace" on its front page. The front page is objective.
explanation: "Disgrace" is a strong opinion, so the front page is subjective.

statement: Two reports on the same election both aim to be objective, but they choose very different photos of the winner. Even objective-sounding reports involve choices.
explanation: Choosing a photo can shape opinion, however neutral the words.

statement: A documentary plays dark, threatening music every time the factory owner appears. The documentary is completely objective about him.
explanation: The music shapes how we feel about him, so it is not objective.

statement: Without the caption "Hero of the flood", a photo of a muddy man could mean anything. The words provide anchorage.
explanation: The caption fixes the meaning we take from the image.

statement: A photo of a crying girl appears with no caption or headline. The image has strong anchorage.
explanation: With no words to fix its meaning, the image is open to many readings.

statement: The same photo of a crowd running is captioned "Fans celebrate" in one paper and "Panic in the streets" in another. The captions anchor opposite meanings.
explanation: The words decide whether we see joy or fear.

statement: A perfume advert shows only a woman walking on a beach, with the slogan "Freedom". The slogan has no effect on how we read the image.
explanation: "Freedom" anchors the image, telling us to see her walk as freeing.

statement: The mise-en-scène of a detective's office, with piles of files and a forgotten coffee, shows how hard he works.
explanation: The objects in the scene tell us about his habits.

statement: A film's music and the speed of its editing are part of its mise-en-scène.
explanation: Mise-en-scène is what is placed in front of the camera; music and editing are added afterwards.

statement: In a teen film, the popular girl's bedroom is all pink, with trophies and mirrors. The mise-en-scène tells us about her before she speaks.
explanation: Her room is designed to show that winning and appearance matter to her.

statement: A director films a tense dinner with a broken chair, a cracked plate and a flickering light. The mise-en-scène suggests a happy, relaxed family.
explanation: Broken and flickering objects suggest tension and things falling apart.

statement: A documentary opens on a scientist's lab, her notebooks and the night sky she studies. These settings and props are not part of the mise-en-scène.
explanation: Settings and props in front of the camera are exactly what mise-en-scène means.

statement: A brand pays a famous actor to say he "always" uses their shampoo. This makes the advert feel more authentic.
explanation: A paid famous actor reading a script can feel less authentic than a real customer.

statement: A charity lets young carers film their own days on their phones. The shaky footage makes the campaign feel more authentic.
explanation: Unpolished footage made by the carers themselves feels real.

statement: A clothing brand stops editing out its models' stretch marks. The aim is to look more authentic.
explanation: Showing real skin suggests honesty.

statement: A travel vlogger films every scene three times to get the perfect "spontaneous" reaction. The reactions are authentic.
explanation: Repeating a "spontaneous" moment makes it a performance, not an authentic reaction.

statement: The smiles in a stock photo look artificial: nobody laughs that hard at a spreadsheet.
explanation: The reaction is far bigger than the situation, so it seems fake.

statement: A documentary shows a farmer's ordinary day with no music and no presenter. A plain approach like this usually makes a documentary feel artificial.
explanation: The plain approach makes it feel natural rather than artificial.

statement: A cereal advert lights its breakfast table perfectly, with no crumbs and no spills. The scene looks artificial.
explanation: Real breakfasts are messy, so perfection seems staged.

statement: A sitcom adds a laughter track that laughs at every joke. A laughter track like this often makes a comedy feel more natural.
explanation: Recorded laughter at every joke is artificial and can feel forced.

statement: After a man uses a new deodorant, crowds chase his car through the city. The advert's picture of the product's effect is realistic.
explanation: The reaction is exaggerated for comic effect.

statement: A cartoon villain has a huge moustache, a booming laugh and a black cape. These exaggerated features tell children at once who the bad guy is.
explanation: Making features bigger and stronger makes the meaning obvious.

statement: A political cartoon draws the prime minister with an enormous nose. The exaggerated feature is meant to mock him.
explanation: Exaggeration is a common way to make fun of someone.

statement: A news report on a small kitchen fire calls it "a disaster that destroyed the town centre". The report gives a careful, accurate account.
explanation: Calling a small fire a disaster is exaggerated.

statement: A school poster about healthy eating divides all food into "good" and "bad". The message is simplified.
explanation: Real nutrition is more complex than two groups.

statement: A documentary spends three hours exploring the causes of a war from many sides. Its picture of the war is simplified.
explanation: Hours of many viewpoints give a detailed, complex picture.

statement: A children's film shows the forest as a simple fight between a kind deer and a cruel hunter. The film gives a simplified picture of nature.
explanation: Real ecosystems are not just good and evil.

statement: A news app sums up a long trial in one sentence. One sentence can capture the full complexity of a trial.
explanation: One sentence must leave out most of the detail, so it is simplified.

statement: A perfume advert is conventional: a beautiful couple, a beach and a slow-motion kiss.
explanation: It follows the usual, expected features of perfume adverts.

statement: A football advert shows only the crowd's faces and never the players or the ball. The advert is very conventional.
explanation: Leaving out the players and the ball is unusual; most football adverts show the action.

statement: A conventional news photo of a politician shows them smiling and shaking hands. This is what audiences expect to see.
explanation: These are familiar features that rarely surprise viewers.

statement: A supermarket's Christmas advert includes snow, a family meal and presents under a tree. The advert breaks the conventions of Christmas adverts.
explanation: Snow, family meals and presents are among the most usual Christmas features.

statement: A fashion magazine puts a farmer, not a film star, on its cover. This is an unconventional choice.
explanation: Fashion covers usually show models or celebrities.

statement: A horror film is set in a dark house at night with creaking doors. Settings like this are usually unconventional for horror.
explanation: Dark houses and creaking doors are among the most common horror settings.

statement: A car advert shows the car only once, for one second, at the end. The advert is unconventional, perhaps to make viewers curious.
explanation: Most car adverts show the car throughout; hiding it is unusual.

statement: A crisp advert shows people eating crisps happily at a party. Its unconventional approach surprises viewers.
explanation: Happy people eating at a party is exactly what we expect.

statement: A news channel shows only the smashed window from a peaceful march of thousands. Its selective footage could make viewers think the whole march was violent.
explanation: One moment out of many can shape the whole picture.

statement: After years of disabled characters being cast as villains, a new film makes its disabled character the villain again. The film offers a counter-stereotype.
explanation: It repeats the old pattern instead of going against it.

statement: A bank advert shows a female engineer leading a site meeting, but the voice-over praises her mainly for "still making it home for bedtime stories". The advert challenges one gender expectation while reinforcing another.
explanation: Her job goes against a stereotype, but judging her by childcare brings back the idea that a woman's real role is at home.

statement: A documentary about a housing estate uses only night-time shots of litter, graffiti and broken lifts. Because every shot is real footage, the representation of the estate is objective.
explanation: Real footage can still be selective. Leaving out daytime life is a choice, and it constructs a negative representation.

statement: A news report on a protest repeatedly calls one side "residents" and the other "activists". These labels may position the audience to see one side as more reasonable.
explanation: "Residents" suggests people with a natural right to be there; "activists" frames the other side as an organised campaign.

statement: A travel brochure describes a village's people as "untouched by time" and shows them only in traditional dress. The tone is admiring, so this cannot be a form of othering.
explanation: Praise can still other: presenting people as timeless and exotic sets them apart from the "modern" reader.

statement: An aspirational car advert never shows the driver's face. Leaving the face out invites viewers to imagine themselves in the driver's seat.
explanation: An unseen driver could be anyone, so the audience is positioned to identify with the role and desire the lifestyle.

statement: A sitcom's only gay character is the witty best friend whose job is to give the heroine advice. Because he is shown positively, the representation avoids stereotype.
explanation: A positive representation can still be stereotypical: the "gay best friend" is a familiar type with no story of his own.

statement: In a children's film, a plain, clever heroine defeats a glamorous, vain queen. The film sets up a binary opposition between intelligence and beauty.
explanation: The two women are defined against each other, as if being clever and being beautiful ruled each other out.

statement: A news website shows a refugee family photographed from above, the parents looking up at the camera. The angle probably makes the family seem powerful and in control.
explanation: A high angle tends to make people look small and vulnerable. It may create sympathy, but it takes power away from them.

statement: A car advert links a bigger car with a happier family and the respect of the neighbours. The advert carries an ideology in which owning more brings a better life.
explanation: It promotes buying as the route to happiness and status.

statement: A sitcom ends every episode with the family reunited around the dinner table, whatever went wrong. The repeated ending supports an ideology that puts the family above everything.
explanation: The structure keeps returning to the family as the answer to every problem.

statement: A news channel calls tax cuts "relief" and tax rises "a burden". These word choices are free of ideology.
explanation: The words frame tax as a weight to be lifted, which reflects a particular political view.

statement: A fashion brand's campaign says "Wear your values" over images of recycled fabric. The brand uses an environmental ideology to sell clothes.
explanation: It links buying the product with green beliefs.

statement: A film celebrates a lone hero who ignores the law to save his town. Its ideology suggests that rules and institutions protect people best.
explanation: It suggests the opposite: that individuals must act when institutions fail.

statement: In a crime drama set in a city, homeless characters appear only as background figures or as suspects. Homeless people are marginalised in the drama.
explanation: They are pushed to the edges of the story and given no voice.

statement: A documentary gives a group of refugee teenagers the whole hour to tell their own stories in their own words. The documentary marginalises them.
explanation: It puts them at the centre and lets them speak, the opposite of marginalising.

statement: A history textbook covers the factory owners of the Industrial Revolution in detail but mentions child workers in only one sentence. The child workers are marginalised.
explanation: They are reduced to a brief mention in a story that was partly theirs.

statement: A city has a large Roma community, but the local news mentions it only in crime stories. Because the community is large, it is unlikely to be marginalised.
explanation: Size does not protect a group; being shown rarely and negatively pushes it to the margins.

statement: A fantasy film's only dark-skinned characters are servants who never speak. The film marginalises them through both role and silence.
explanation: They are given low status and no voice.

statement: A sports channel shows women's football late at night, after the men's highlights. The scheduling gives women's football a central place.
explanation: Late-night slots after the men's game push it to the margins.

statement: A news report describes a festival held by an immigrant community as "strange rituals" full of "exotic smells". The language is othering.
explanation: Words like "strange" and "exotic" present the community as alien to "us".

statement: A documentary about a remote village lets the villagers explain their own customs in their own language, with subtitles. The documentary others the villagers.
explanation: Letting them explain themselves treats them as people with their own voice, not as strange outsiders.

statement: A video game's enemies all speak an invented, foreign-sounding language and are never given names. The game others its enemies.
explanation: Making them nameless and foreign marks them as alien and easy to fight.

statement: A science fiction film gives its aliens the same fears, jokes and family worries as the humans. The film's representation of the aliens is a clear example of othering.
explanation: Giving the aliens human feelings makes them familiar, which works against othering.

statement: A newspaper calls asylum seekers "a swarm" arriving on the coast. The word choice others them by comparing people to insects.
